# Architecture Design {.unnumbered}

The PoC taught us how the hardware behaves. It also showed the limits of a single sketch: every feature lives in `setup()`, nothing can be tested without the board, and each new feature makes the file harder to change.

Before writing any code, this chapter designs the new firmware on paper: what it must do, how it decides what to do at each wake-up, how it is split into modules, how we will check that it works, and how it reacts to failures. The following chapters implement this design step by step.

## Requirements

Requirements come in two kinds:

- **Functional requirements** (F) describe *what* the station does: measure, store, upload.
- **Non-functional requirements** (N) describe *how well* it must do it: without losing data, without running out of battery, while remaining testable and extensible.

Each requirement has an identifier, a short name, and the reason why it exists. Each one also comes with an **acceptance criterion**: a measurable condition that tells us whether the firmware meets it. These criteria are listed in the [verification matrix](#verification-matrix), together with the way each one is checked.

### Functional requirements

| ID | Name | Requirement | Why |
|----|----------|--------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| F1 | Periodic measurement | Measure temperature, humidity and pressure every 15 minutes, on a fixed UTC grid (`:00`, `:15`, `:30`, `:45`). | Regular, aligned measurements are what the dashboard and the forecasting model (Phase 6) expect, and they make days easy to compare. |
| F2 | Store first | Append every measurement to the SD card before any network activity. | The SD card is the source of truth. If the upload fails or the firmware crashes during the Wi-Fi connection, the measurement is already safe. |
| F3 | Hourly upload | Once per hour, upload the rows that the server has not received yet, over the home Wi-Fi. | The dashboard and the short-term forecast need data less than one hour old, and uploading more often would cost too much energy (see N3). |
| F4 | Daily time sync | Synchronize the RTC with NTP once every 24 hours, reusing an upload connection. | The DS3231 drifts by about one minute per year. A daily correction is more than enough, and reusing an existing connection costs almost nothing. |
| F5 | Maintenance mode | When the button is pressed, start a Wi-Fi access point for 3 minutes, with a web page to download or delete the data. | It allows retrieving the data when the home Wi-Fi is out of reach, without opening the enclosure. |
| F6 | Flag unreliable time | When the clock is not reliable, keep measuring, but flag the rows. | We keep the data (N1) without silently mixing wrong timestamps with correct ones. |

### Non-functional requirements

| ID | Name | Requirement | Why |
|----|----------|--------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| N1 | No data loss | A Wi-Fi, server or NTP failure never loses a measurement, and a sensor failure never stops the schedule. | Collecting data is the purpose of the station. An upload can always be retried later, but a missed measurement is lost for good. |
| N2 | Always wake up again | The station never goes to sleep without a way to wake up. | Outdoors, a station stuck in deep sleep stops collecting silently: nobody notices until someone checks the data, possibly weeks later. |
| N3 | Energy | Use Wi-Fi at most once per hour in normal operation, and keep a measurement-only wake-up to about one second. | Wi-Fi is by far the largest consumer. According to the [Power Budget](../../PoC/Phase-03/05-power-budget.qmd#cost-of-wi-fi), hourly uploads give about 8 months on a 2000 mAh battery, versus about 3 months when uploading at every measurement. |
| N4 | Testability | All decision logic can be tested on a computer, without hardware. | Many situations are hard or slow to reproduce on the bench: Wi-Fi down exactly at a full hour, RTC power loss, full SD card. On a computer, each one becomes a repeatable test that runs in milliseconds. |
| N5 | Extensibility | Adding a sensor means writing a new adapter and adding a column, without changing the state machine. | Phases 7 to 10 add light, UV, soil moisture, rain and wind sensors. Each addition must not risk breaking the logic that already works. |

## Design Invariants

These rules hold everywhere in the firmware:

| Topic | Rule |
|-------|------|
| Time | All times are Unix timestamps in **UTC**. The DS3231 is the only time source used for timestamps. |
| Source of truth | The **SD card** holds every measurement. The server only receives copies. |
| Wake-up model | Each wake-up is a fresh boot that runs the state machine once, from `BOOT` to `SLEEP`. |
| Missing values | A value that could not be measured is stored as an **empty field**, never as a fake number. |
| Hardware access | Only *adapters* talk to the hardware. The decision logic never calls Arduino or ESP-IDF functions. |

## Data Format (v1)

Measurements are appended to `/measurements_v1.csv`, one row per wake-up:

```csv
timestamp,time_valid,temperature_c,humidity_pct,pressure_hpa
2026-10-01T14:15:00Z,1,18.42,62.10,1013.20
2026-10-01T14:30:00Z,1,18.37,,1013.18
```

- `timestamp`: ISO 8601 in UTC, with the explicit `Z` suffix.
- `time_valid`: `1` if the clock was reliable when the row was written, `0` otherwise (F6 · Flag unreliable time).
- The column names now include their unit, so the file can be read without documentation.
- The second row shows a missing humidity value (empty field).

A row is about 50 bytes: 96 rows per day represent about 5 KB per day, less than 2 MB per year.

When new sensors are added, the file format changes: the firmware then writes to a new file (`measurements_v2.csv`) with the new columns. A file never mixes two formats.

## Persistent Context

Deep sleep erases the RAM, but some information must survive between wake-ups. Each piece is stored where its lifetime makes sense:

| Information | Stored in | Lost when | Consequence if lost |
|-------------|-----------|-----------|---------------------|
| Current time | DS3231 | Coin cell removed or empty | Clock invalid until the next NTP sync |
| Clock validity | DS3231 *Oscillator Stop Flag* | Never: this flag *is* the record of a power loss | — |
| Upload cursor (position of the first row not yet uploaded) | SD card, `/upload.idx` | SD card replaced | Everything is uploaded again (harmless, see [Upload Protocol](#upload-protocol)) |
| Time of the last NTP sync | RTC memory (`RTC_DATA_ATTR`) | ESP32 power loss or reset | An extra NTP sync at the next upload |

The clock validity needs no extra storage. As seen in Phase 01, the DS3231 sets its *Oscillator Stop Flag* when it loses power, and `rtc.adjust()` clears it. So the clock is reliable if and only if the flag is clear. When it is set, the station keeps running on whatever time the RTC holds, and marks its rows with `time_valid = 0` until NTP succeeds.

## State Machine

At each wake-up, the firmware runs through the following states:

| State | Role |
|-------|------|
| `BOOT` | Initialize the buses, read the wake-up cause and the clock status. |
| `MEASURE` | Read all sensors (missing values stay empty). |
| `STORE` | Append the row to the SD card. |
| `UPLOAD` | Connect to Wi-Fi and send the rows after the upload cursor. |
| `TIME_SYNC` | Correct the RTC with NTP, using the open connection. |
| `MAINTENANCE` | Run the access point and web page for 3 minutes. |
| `SCHEDULE` | Program the next RTC alarm on the 15-minute grid. |
| `SLEEP` | Arm the wake-up sources and enter deep sleep. |

```{mermaid}
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> BOOT
    BOOT --> MAINTENANCE : woken by the button
    BOOT --> MEASURE : woken by the alarm, the timer, or power-on
    MAINTENANCE --> MEASURE : after 3 minutes
    MEASURE --> STORE : always
    STORE --> UPLOAD : upload needed
    STORE --> SCHEDULE : no upload needed
    UPLOAD --> TIME_SYNC : Wi-Fi connected and sync needed
    UPLOAD --> SCHEDULE : no Wi-Fi, or no sync needed
    TIME_SYNC --> SCHEDULE : always
    SCHEDULE --> SLEEP : always
    SLEEP --> [*]
```

"Always" means that the state moves on once its work is done, whether it succeeded or not: failures are handled inside the state, as described in [Error Handling](#error-handling). Here is the complete list of transitions:

| From | To | Condition |
|------|----|-----------|
| `BOOT` | `MAINTENANCE` | The wake-up cause is the button (`EXT1`). |
| `BOOT` | `MEASURE` | Any other cause: RTC alarm (`EXT0`), safety timer, or power-on. |
| `MAINTENANCE` | `MEASURE` | The 3-minute session is over. |
| `MEASURE` | `STORE` | Always. |
| `STORE` | `UPLOAD` | **upload needed** is true. |
| `STORE` | `SCHEDULE` | **upload needed** is false. |
| `UPLOAD` | `TIME_SYNC` | The Wi-Fi connection succeeded **and** **sync needed** is true. |
| `UPLOAD` | `SCHEDULE` | The Wi-Fi connection failed, **or** **sync needed** is false: every case except the one above. |
| `TIME_SYNC` | `SCHEDULE` | Always. |
| `SCHEDULE` | `SLEEP` | Always. |

The transitions out of `STORE` and `UPLOAD` depend on two conditions, computed by pure functions that can be tested on a computer:

| Condition | True when… |
|-----------|------------|
| **upload needed** | The current measurement belongs to a full-hour slot (`:00`), **or** the clock is invalid. In the second case, the station tries to reach NTP at every wake-up until the clock is valid again. |
| **sync needed** | The clock is invalid, **or** the last NTP sync is more than 24 hours old. |

The first condition tests the *slot* of the measurement, not its exact time. The firmware reads the clock a few seconds after the alarm (or 60 seconds after it, when woken by the safety timer), so a measurement is never taken at exactly `14:00:00`. The time is first rounded down to the 15-minute grid ($t - (t \bmod T)$, see below): `14:00:03` and `14:01:00` both belong to the `14:00` slot, which is a full hour.

### Computing the next alarm

`SCHEDULE` programs the alarm for the next slot of the 15-minute grid, strictly after the current time:

$$t_{next} = t_{now} - (t_{now} \bmod T) + T \qquad \text{with } T = 15 \times 60 = 900\,s$$

$T$ is the measurement interval of F1 · Periodic measurement, in seconds, since Unix timestamps count seconds. The term $t_{now} \bmod T$ is the time elapsed since the last slot. For example, at `14:07:23`, 443 seconds have elapsed since `14:00:00`, so $t_{next} = $ `14:07:23` $-$ 443 s $+$ 900 s $=$ `14:15:00`. In the code, $T$ is a field of the `Config` structure of the core, not a hard-coded 900.

### Two design choices

- **`MAINTENANCE` goes to `MEASURE`, not to `SLEEP`.** An alarm may have fired during the 3-minute session. Instead of handling this case separately, we always take a reading after a maintenance session. It costs one extra row, and `SCHEDULE` then realigns the station on the grid.
- **`SCHEDULE` always recomputes the alarm from the current time.** It never reuses a time read earlier in the wake-up, so an alarm can never be set in the past (the bug fixed in the PoC).

## Modules and Interfaces

### Why split the firmware?

Two of our requirements cannot be met by a single sketch:

- **N4 · Testability** asks that the decisions be tested on a computer. We want to check most acceptance criteria above (F1 to F4, F6, N1 to N3) *before* flashing the board, and in situations that are hard to reproduce on the bench.
- **N5 · Extensibility** asks that a sensor can be added without touching the logic.

In the PoC, the same lines of code make decisions ("is it time to upload?") and drive the hardware (`WiFi.begin()`, `SD.open()`). A decision cannot be tested without the whole station, and changing a component means editing the logic.

The usual solution is to separate the code into layers that only communicate through **interfaces**. This approach is known as *ports and adapters* (or *hexagonal architecture*).

### The three layers

**Core**
:   The state machine, the rules (*upload needed*, *sync needed*, next alarm) and the CSV row format. It never talks to the hardware, and it is tested on the computer.

**Interfaces**
:   The list of services the core needs, in its own terms: read the time, read the sensors, store a row, send data, go to sleep. They only *declare* functions; they contain no code.

**Adapters**
:   One implementation of each interface for the real hardware, using the existing libraries (RTClib, Adafruit BME280, SD, WiFi, HTTPClient). They are tested on the board.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    core["Core logic<br/>state machine, rules, CSV format"]
    ports["Interfaces<br/>IClock, ISensor, IStorage, INetwork,<br/>IPower, IMaintenance"]
    hw["Hardware adapters<br/>DS3231, BME280, SD card, Wi-Fi,<br/>access point, ESP32 sleep"]
    doubles["Test doubles<br/>fake clock, fake sensor, ..."]
    core -- uses --> ports
    hw -. implements .-> ports
    doubles -. implements .-> ports
```

The core only knows the interfaces. On the board, `main.cpp` gives it the hardware adapters. In the tests, we give it **test doubles** instead: simple implementations whose behavior the test controls (see [Verification Strategy](#verification-strategy)).

### What an interface looks like

In C++, an interface is a class that only declares functions, without implementing them (*pure virtual* functions, marked `= 0`). Here is what the core needs from a clock:

```cpp
// What the core needs from a clock, and nothing more
class IClock {
public:
    virtual ~IClock() = default;
    virtual uint32_t now() = 0;                 // Unix time, UTC
    virtual bool isValid() = 0;                 // false after a power loss
    virtual void setTime(uint32_t unixTime) = 0;
    virtual bool setAlarm(uint32_t unixTime) = 0; // false if not set
};
```

This interface does not mention I2C, registers or RTClib. It has two implementations:

- `Ds3231Clock`, for the board: `now()` returns `rtc.now().unixtime()`, `isValid()` returns `!rtc.lostPower()`, and so on.
- `FakeClock`, for the tests: `now()` returns a number that the test sets, and `setAlarm()` just records the requested time so the test can check it.

The state machine receives an `IClock&` and cannot tell which one it is using. The other interfaces follow the same pattern: `ISensor` (read a measurement), `IStorage` (append a row, read rows after the cursor, move the cursor), `INetwork` (connect, send a batch, get the NTP time), `IPower` (read the wake-up cause, sleep with the given wake-up sources) and `IMaintenance` (run the access point session).

`IClock` is enough to show the principle here. The complete code of all the interfaces is given in the first chapter of step A1, [Interfaces and State Machine](01-1-interfaces-and-state-machine.qmd#the-interfaces), where it is included directly from the repository.

### Project layout

The project is a single PlatformIO project with two environments: `esp32` builds the firmware for the board, and `native` builds the core and the tests for the computer.

```text
firmware/paws/
├── platformio.ini      # [env:esp32] for the board, [env:native] for tests
├── include/
│   └── secrets.example.h   # Wi-Fi and server settings (step A4)
├── lib/
│   ├── core/           # Config, rules, state machine, CSV format
│   │                   # (no Arduino)
│   └── ports/          # interfaces and the data they exchange
├── src/
│   ├── adapters/       # hardware implementations (pins at the top)
│   └── main.cpp        # creates the adapters and runs the state machine
└── test/
    ├── doubles/        # test doubles, shared by all tests
    ├── test_rules/     # unit tests
    └── test_scenarios/ # scenario tests
```

## Verification Strategy {#verification-strategy}

Each requirement is checked by at least one test. We use three levels of tests:

**Unit tests**
:   Check **one function in isolation**, with chosen inputs. For example: the next alarm after `14:07:23` is `14:15:00`, and the next alarm after exactly `14:15:00` is `14:30:00` (strictly after). They run on the computer.

**Scenario tests**
:   Run **the whole state machine** with test doubles, and check an acceptance criterion. For example, for N1 · No data loss: at `14:00:00`, with the Wi-Fi down, the row is stored, the upload cursor does not move, the next alarm is `14:15:00`, and the machine reaches `SLEEP`. A scenario can also simulate a whole day in a loop (96 wake-ups) to check F3 · Hourly upload or N3 · Energy. They run on the computer.

**Board tests**
:   Check **the adapters** on the real hardware, with a checklist of expected serial output (as in the PoC chapters). They cannot run automatically, since the CI has no ESP32, so they are done by hand at each step.

Unit and scenario tests use [Unity](https://github.com/ThrowTheSwitch/Unity), the C unit-test framework integrated in PlatformIO. They run with `pio test -e native` and are added to the CI, so every pull request is checked automatically. The framework is set up in step A1, with the first tests.

### Verification matrix {#verification-matrix}

This table gives, for each requirement, its acceptance criterion and the level of test that checks it. It links the requirements to the tests: when a test fails, we know which requirement is at risk.

| Requirement | Acceptance criterion | Verified by |
|----|--------------------------------------------|--------------|
| F1 · Periodic measurement | Every alarm programmed by the firmware falls on a 15-minute slot, strictly in the future. | Unit + scenario |
| F2 · Store first | In every scenario, the row is written to storage before any network call. | Scenario (mock) |
| F3 · Hourly upload | Over a simulated day with Wi-Fi available, exactly 24 uploads take place, and after each one, the server has received every row stored before it. | Scenario (simulated day) |
| F4 · Daily time sync | Over three simulated days, exactly three synchronizations take place, and none of them opens its own Wi-Fi connection. | Scenario (simulated days) |
| F5 · Maintenance mode | On the board, the access point appears after a button press, the CSV file can be downloaded, and the station goes back to its normal cycle after 3 minutes. | Board |
| F6 · Flag unreliable time | Rows written while the clock is invalid have `time_valid = 0`, and rows written after a successful NTP sync have `time_valid = 1`. | Scenario |
| N1 · No data loss | In every failure scenario (Wi-Fi down, server error, NTP down, sensor missing), the storage contains one row per wake-up, and the upload cursor never moves past a row that the server has not acknowledged. | Scenario (failure cases) |
| N2 · Always wake up again | In every scenario, including an RTC failure, the station goes to sleep with the safety timer armed, in addition to the RTC alarm when the RTC works. | Scenario |
| N3 · Energy | Over a simulated day with a valid clock, at most 24 Wi-Fi connections are opened. On the board, the awake time printed by the firmware before sleeping (measured with `millis()`, no instrument needed) stays below 1.5 seconds for a measurement-only wake-up. | Scenario (simulated day) + board |
| N4 · Testability | The core logic compiles for the computer without any Arduino header, and all tests run automatically on every pull request. | CI |
| N5 · Extensibility | When the first new sensor is added (Phase 7), no file of the state machine is modified. | Review (Phase 7) |

Most criteria are checked by scenario tests on the computer. Only F5 (which needs the access point and a phone) and part of N3 (the real awake time) require the board, and N5 can only be checked when a new sensor is actually added.

### Test doubles

A *test double* replaces a real component during a test, like a stunt double replaces an actor. There are several kinds, depending on what the test needs:

| Kind | What it does | Example in PAWS |
|------|--------------|-----------------|
| **Stub** | Returns fixed answers, and nothing else. | A sensor that always returns 18.4 °C, 62 %, 1013 hPa. |
| **Fake** | A simplified but working implementation. | A storage that keeps rows in RAM instead of the SD card; a clock whose time the test sets and advances. |
| **Mock** | Records the calls it receives, so the test can check them (which calls, in which order, with which arguments). | A network that records each `connect()`, to check that the row was stored *before* (F2 · Store first). |
| **Fixture** | Not a double, but the common setup shared by several tests. | "A station at 14:00, with a valid clock, an empty storage and a working Wi-Fi." |

We write these doubles by hand: each one is a few lines implementing an interface. Mocking libraries exist (such as GoogleMock), but they add a dependency and complexity that our small interfaces do not need.

## Upload Protocol {#upload-protocol}

The PoC sent the whole CSV file at every upload, and the dummy server overwrote its copy each time. This protocol replaces it with three goals: send only the new rows, never lose data (N1), and survive an interruption at any moment. It is also the **contract with the Phase 5 backend**.

### The upload cursor

The station remembers where the server's copy ends with an **upload cursor**: the position, in bytes, of the first row of `/measurements_v1.csv` that the server has not acknowledged yet. It is stored in the small file `/upload.idx` on the SD card, so it survives power losses.

We use a position in bytes rather than a row number because the SD adapter can then jump directly to it (`file.seek()`), without reading the whole file. The cursor always points to the beginning of a row.

### Request

The station sends the rows after the cursor, preceded by the header line, so that each request is self-describing:

```http
POST /api/v1/measurements HTTP/1.1
Host: 192.168.1.15:8000
Content-Type: text/csv

timestamp,time_valid,temperature_c,humidity_pct,pressure_hpa
2026-10-01T13:15:00Z,1,18.20,63.40,1013.35
2026-10-01T13:30:00Z,1,18.31,62.90,1013.28
2026-10-01T13:45:00Z,1,18.35,62.50,1013.22
2026-10-01T14:00:00Z,1,18.40,62.20,1013.21
```

A request contains at most **500 rows** (about 25 KB). This bounds the duration of each request and the memory needed on the server. In normal operation, an upload contains 4 rows. After a week without Wi-Fi, the 672 missing rows are sent in two requests.

### Response

The server stores the rows and **ignores rows whose timestamp already exists**. It answers with a `2xx` status code and a short JSON summary:

```json
{"received": 4, "inserted": 4, "duplicates": 0}
```

The station only relies on the status code. The summary is printed on the serial port, which helps debugging.

### Sequence

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Station
    participant SD as SD card
    participant B as Backend
    S->>SD: Read the cursor and the next rows (at most 500)
    S->>B: POST /api/v1/measurements (header + rows)
    B-->>S: 200 OK {"received": 500, ...}
    S->>SD: Move the cursor after the sent rows
    S->>SD: Read the next rows
    S->>B: POST /api/v1/measurements (header + rows)
    B-->>S: 200 OK {"received": 172, ...}
    S->>SD: Move the cursor after the sent rows
    Note over S,SD: No rows left: the upload is complete
```

### Failure cases

The protocol relies on two rules: **the cursor only moves forward after a `2xx` response**, and **the server accepts duplicates without error**. Together, they cover every interruption:

| What happens | Result |
|--------------|--------|
| The Wi-Fi connection fails | Nothing is sent; the cursor does not move; retry at the next full hour. |
| The server answers with an error (not `2xx`) | The cursor does not move; the same rows are sent at the next upload. |
| The server stores the rows, but the response is lost (timeout, Wi-Fi drop) | The cursor does not move; the rows are sent again at the next upload, and the server ignores them as duplicates. |
| Power loss after the response, before the cursor is written | Same as a lost response: the rows are sent again and ignored. |
| `/upload.idx` is lost or unreadable | The cursor restarts at the beginning of the file: everything is sent again, and the server ignores the duplicates. |

In every case, the rows remain on the SD card, and the server never stores a row twice in its database. This property, where repeating a request has the same effect as sending it once, is called **idempotence**.

One case is not solved automatically: if the server keeps rejecting the same batch (for example because of a malformed row caused by a bug), the uploads are blocked. The data is still safe on the SD card, and the problem is visible on the dashboard, since no new data arrives.

### Scope

The protocol uses plain HTTP on the home network, without authentication, consistent with the single-user scope defined in [Motivation & Goals](../../01-motivation.qmd). It would need encryption (HTTPS) and authentication if the server were ever exposed to the internet.

## Error Handling {#error-handling}

| Failure | Behavior |
|---------|----------|
| BME280 not responding | The row is stored with empty values; the schedule continues. |
| SD card missing or full | The measurement is lost (reported on the serial port); the schedule continues. |
| Wi-Fi not reachable within 10 s | No upload; the cursor does not move; retry at the next full hour. |
| Server error or timeout | Same as above. |
| NTP not answering within 5 s | Retry at the next upload. |
| RTC not responding | Timestamps and alarms are impossible: the rows are flagged invalid, and the ESP32 internal timer wakes the station up (see below). |
| Firmware stuck | The ESP32 watchdog resets the chip; the next boot takes a reading and goes back to the normal cycle. |

To guarantee N2 · Always wake up again, `SLEEP` always arms **three** wake-up sources:

1. the DS3231 alarm (`EXT0`, GPIO 36), the normal source;
2. the button (`EXT1`, GPIO 39);
3. the ESP32 internal timer, as a safety net: it is set to fire **60 seconds after** the planned alarm (or after 15 minutes if the RTC cannot be read). Even with the timer's drift of a few percent, the RTC alarm always fires first when it works. If the RTC fails, the station keeps waking up roughly every 15 minutes instead of sleeping forever. A wake-up by the timer is handled like an alarm.

## Energy Estimate

With the method and assumptions of the [Power Budget](../../PoC/Phase-03/05-power-budget.qmd) chapter (estimates, not measurements):

| Item | Average current |
|------|-----------------|
| Deep sleep (modules, no LED) + 96 measurement wake-ups per day | ~0.18 mA |
| 24 uploads per day (~5 s at 120 mA each) | ~0.17 mA |
| **Total** | **~0.35 mA**, i.e. about 8 months on a 2000 mAh battery |

The daily NTP sync is negligible, since it reuses an upload connection.

## Implementation Plan

The implementation is split into six steps, numbered A1 to A6 (A for Architecture). Each step is a chapter of the book, a tag in the repository, and a working firmware:

| Step | Content | Hardware needed |
|------|---------|-----------------|
| A1 | Project skeleton, interfaces, state machine, test doubles, Unity setup and first tests | None |
| A2 | DS3231 clock adapter and scheduling rules (grid, safety timer) | ESP32 + DS3231 |
| A3 | BME280 and SD card adapters, CSV v1 format | + BME280 + SD |
| A4 | Wi-Fi, incremental upload with cursor, NTP sync | + Wi-Fi |
| A5 | Maintenance mode (button, access point, web page) | + button |
| A6 | Hardening: watchdog, error handling review, updated power estimate | Full station |

The next chapter, [Interfaces and State Machine](01-1-interfaces-and-state-machine.qmd), starts step A1.
